section_summary: This section continues a wide-ranging survey of Philippine history and society, moving from the Spanish colonial legacy and the revolution through American conquest, administration, and the promised transition to independence. It then describes the archipelago’s settlement patterns, regional and linguistic diversity, migration, cities, and agricultural economy, supported by maps and population statistics. The closing chapters contrast relatively favorable frontier tenancy in the Cagayan Valley with the indebted, coercive hacienda system of Nueva Ecija and explain the resulting agrarian unrest.

subfiles.title: [Survey of the Philippines: Spanish heritage, American rule, population, diversity, and agrarian life, pp. 29–77]
subfiles.about: An extended social-scientific survey traces Philippine historical development and examines population, cultural diversity, agriculture, tenancy, and the sources of agrarian conflict.
subfiles.summary: The excerpt begins in the middle of a historical chapter and describes the effects of Spanish rule, Filipino nationalism, Rizal’s martyrdom, and the revolutionary leadership of Aguinaldo and Mabini. It then recounts the American conquest and civil administration, educational and economic policies, changing degrees of Filipino self-government, and the 1934 transition toward independence. Subsequent chapters use maps, statistics, and descriptive journeys to examine uneven settlement, migration, foreign communities, regional ethnic and linguistic groups, and the development of a broader Filipino national identity. The final portion analyzes agricultural poverty through contrasting accounts of the frontier tenant Adoy in the Cagayan Valley and an indebted hacienda tenant in Nueva Ecija, ending amid a discussion of agrarian discontent and cacique power.
